chunks: From him, from Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Dawud al-Nahdi, from some of our companions, who said:

Ibn Abi Sa'id al-Mukari entered upon Abu al-Hasan al-Rida (peace be upon him) and said to him, 'I ask you about a matter.' He said, 'I do not think you will accept from me, and you are not from my flock, but bring it forth.'
A man said, 'He said, 'At my death, every slave of mine who is 'qadeem' (old/long-held) is free for the sake of Allah, the Exalted.'
Until it becomes like an old (crooked) stalk.
So any of his slaves who had been with him for six months, he is 'qadeem' and free.
He said, 'So he went out and became poor until he died, and he did not have enough for a night's lodging. May Allah curse him.'

key_terms.ابْنُ أَبِي سَعِيدٍ الْمُكَارِي: Ibn Abi Sa'id al-Mukari, a companion known for his wealth and subsequent poverty
key_terms.الْعُرْجُونِ الْقَدِيمِ: The old stalk, a Quranic phrase used here as a linguistic basis for the legal definition
key_terms.سِتَّةُ أَشْهُرٍ: Six months, the specific duration defined by the Imam for a slave to be considered 'qadeem'
key_terms.قَدِيمٌ: Old or long-held, a technical term in this hadith referring to the duration of ownership
key_terms.لِوَجْهِ اللَّهِ: For the sake of Allah, indicating the spiritual intent behind the act of emancipation

ai.seo_question: What is the definition of 'qadeem' (old) slaves in Shia jurisprudence regarding emancipation?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* clarifies the legal definition of 'qadeem' (long-held) slaves for emancipation purposes, with Imam al-Rida (AS) citing the Quranic phrase 'al-'urjun al-qadim' to establish a six-month duration. The narrative highlights the practical application of this ruling by Ibn Abi Sa'id al-Mukari, whose subsequent poverty and the narrator's curse upon him serve as a cautionary tale regarding the financial prudence of immediate, total emancipation.
